items.prompt: What does a codebase reliably tell you about a past decision?
choices: Why it was chosen over the alternatives
items.explanation: Code shows the outcome. The reasoning behind it is not stored in it.

items.prompt: What does ADR stand for?
items.explanation: An ADR is a record of one architecture decision.

items.prompt: How many decisions should one ADR capture?
choices: Every decision for a whole system
All decisions made in a quarter
Only the decisions that turned out wrong
items.explanation: Each ADR is a single decision, written once.

items.prompt: Where does undocumented reasoning mostly live?
choices: In people's memory and chat threads
items.explanation: Without a record, reasoning exists only as long as the people and threads do.

items.prompt: When people who made a decision leave and nothing was written, what is lost first?
items.explanation: The code stays; the why is what disappears.

items.prompt: Why is a one-line 'we chose X' weak as a record?
choices: It says what but not why
items.explanation: The why is the valuable part and is exactly what the one-liner omits.

items.prompt: A new team wants to change an inherited technology choice. What do they need to know first?
choices: Why it was chosen in the first place
How many lines of code it has
items.explanation: Without the original reasoning they risk repeating a migration that was already rejected.

items.prompt: How long does an ADR need to be useful?
choices: As long as a full design document
Long enough to cover every future change
Short enough to read in minutes, durable for years
items.explanation: Short and durable is the point: five minutes of reading instead of a week of archaeology.

items.prompt: A team inherits a service built on a technology nobody understands the reason for. Searching commit history shows many commits about what changed but none about why. What is the best explanation of why history cannot answer the question?
choices: Commits record changes, not the alternatives that were weighed and the constraints that ruled them out
Commit history is always deleted after a year, as most teams assume in practice
Commit messages are limited to too few characters, which is the usual convention
Only code reviewers can read old commits, since that is how it is normally done
items.explanation: Version history is a log of what changed. The rejected options and the constraints were discussed elsewhere and never written down.
items.reference:
💻 Code — shows what the system does today
🧠 Reasoning — what was considered and rejected lives in heads and chat threads
📄 ADR — a durable record of one decision and why

Why: code records outcomes, not the alternatives and constraints behind them, so the why leaves with the people.
items.reflection: Think of a rule or habit in your family, school, or workplace that nobody can explain anymore. What would a one-paragraph note, written when it started, have saved people since?

items.prompt: Two proposals for preserving architectural reasoning: (A) a short per-decision record kept in the repo, (B) a single long design document for the entire system, updated occasionally. Which is the better fit for the problem a decision record solves, and why?
choices: B, because one document is easier to keep consistent than many small ones, regardless of how circumstances develop
A, because each decision keeps its own context and can be superseded without rewriting everything else
B, because long documents contain more reasoning, as most teams assume in practice
A, because short documents never go out of date, which is the usual convention
items.explanation: Per-decision records stay small and independently correctable. A monolithic document hides which parts are still true.
items.reference:

items.prompt: The engineers who chose a queue technology are still at the company and remember everything. Does the team still gain from writing an ADR?
choices: No, because the knowledge is already safe, since that is how it is normally done
No, because ADRs are only for departed employees, regardless of how circumstances develop
Yes, because memory is not shared, searchable, or permanent, and those people will eventually leave or forget
Yes, but only if a manager requests it, as most teams assume in practice
items.explanation: People are a fragile store. The record outlives their availability, and it also lets newcomers learn without interrupting them.

items.prompt: A migration to a new queue is proposed. Which question would an ADR for the original choice answer fastest?
choices: How many messages per second does the queue handle today?
Which engineer wrote the producer code?, which is the usual convention
What is the queue vendor's market share?, since that is how it is normally done
Was this alternative already considered, and what ruled it out?
items.explanation: The unique value of an ADR is the rejected-alternatives record, which no runtime metric or code reading can provide.

items.prompt: Which ADR section answers 'what problem forced a decision at all?'
items.explanation: Context records the problem and constraints.

items.prompt: Which section states what was actually chosen?
items.explanation: The Decision section is the choice itself.

items.prompt: Which section records trade-offs, both good and bad?
items.explanation: Consequences list what is gained and what is given up.

items.prompt: Which section says whether the decision still applies?
items.explanation: Status marks the decision's lifecycle stage.

items.prompt: Which part do teams most often skip?
items.explanation: Consequences feel optional but carry the most value later.

items.prompt: An optional extra section lists the options that lost. What is it called?
items.explanation: Recording rejected options stops them from being re-proposed.

items.prompt: A status of 'Accepted' means what?
choices: The decision is only a draft
items.explanation: Accepted is the live, in-effect state.

items.prompt: Which status says a newer ADR replaced this one?
items.explanation: Superseded points forward to the replacing record.

items.prompt: An ADR reads: 'Decision: we use PostgreSQL. Status: Accepted.' with no other text. Which missing section hurts a future reader most?
choices: Context and consequences, because they hold the why and the trade-offs
Title, because it is the only way to find it, regardless of how circumstances develop
A link to PostgreSQL's website, as most teams assume in practice
The author's job title, which is the usual convention
items.explanation: The decision alone is what the code already shows. The context and trade-offs are what the reader cannot recover.
items.reference:
🧩 Context — the problem and constraints that forced a choice
✅ Decision — what was actually chosen
⚖️ Consequences — trade-offs, good and bad
🚦 Status — proposed, accepted, superseded, deprecated

Why: each part answers a different question a future reader will ask; skipping consequences removes the most useful one.
items.reflection: Imagine explaining a big purchase or a move to someone years later. Which of context, decision, consequences, and status would they miss most if you left it out, and why?

items.prompt: A draft ADR's Consequences section says only: 'This will make the system better and faster.' What is wrong with it?
choices: It is too short to be accepted, since that is how it is normally done
It lists no trade-offs or costs, so it reads as advocacy and hides what was given up
It should name the author, regardless of how circumstances develop
It belongs in the Context section, as most teams assume in practice
items.explanation: A consequence section must be honest about downsides, not just justify the winner.
items.reference:

✅ Decision — what was actually chosen
⚖️ Consequences — trade-offs, good and bad
🚦 Status — proposed, accepted, superseded, deprecated

Why: each part answers a different question a future reader will ask; skipping consequences removes the most useful one.

items.prompt: Which of these sentences belongs in Context rather than Decision?
choices: We will use the existing RabbitMQ cluster, which is the usual convention
We will add a new vhost for this service, since that is how it is normally done
Roughly 3% of payloads exceed the managed service's 256KB limit
We will revisit if payload rates drop, regardless of how circumstances develop
items.explanation: A fact about the situation that forces the choice is context. The other lines are the decision or consequences.

items.prompt: An engineer finds an ADR with Status 'Accepted' for a technology the team replaced last year. Which part of the record failed?
choices: Context, because it was written before the migration, as most teams assume in practice
Decision, because it named the wrong technology originally, which is the usual convention
Consequences, because they were too detailed, since that is how it is normally done
Status, because it no longer reflects reality and nobody updated or superseded it
items.explanation: The original content can be accurate and historical. A wrong status is what misleads.

items.prompt: Should every decision get an ADR?
choices: Only decisions over a certain code size
items.explanation: Writing one for everything buries the ones that matter.

items.prompt: Which is more likely to deserve an ADR: choosing a primary datastore or choosing a minor-version bump of a logging library?
items.explanation: A datastore shapes everything built on it and is costly to undo.

items.prompt: Which two traits together suggest an ADR?
items.explanation: Both conditions together justify the writing cost.

items.prompt: What is the main cost of writing an ADR for trivial choices?
choices: It buries the decisions that matter in noise
items.explanation: Noise reduces the chance the important records get read.

items.prompt: Choosing an authentication approach for a product is usually...
items.explanation: Authentication shapes many other parts and is costly to change.

items.prompt: Renaming a local variable is usually...
items.explanation: Trivial and instantly reversible.

items.prompt: Who is the typical reader an ADR is written for?
choices: A future team member who wasn't in the room
items.explanation: ADRs outlive the people who made the decision.

items.prompt: The test for whether to write one asks about the decision's...
items.explanation: Significance and cost of reversal decide it.

items.prompt: A team debates two choices: (1) which message broker to use for all inter-service traffic, (2) the file naming scheme in one internal script folder. Which one needs an ADR, and what is the deciding factor?
choices: The broker, because it shapes other systems and is expensive to reverse
The naming scheme, because naming is always contentious, regardless of how circumstances develop
Both, because every disagreement should be recorded, as most teams assume in practice
Neither, because ADRs are only for security, which is the usual convention
items.explanation: Significance and reversal cost decide it, not how much people argue.
items.reference:
📌 Significant — shapes how other parts of the system get built
🔒 Hard to reverse — undoing it means real rework
✍️ Both true — write an ADR
🏃 Otherwise — just make the call

Why: an ADR costs time to write and to read; spending it only on significant, costly-to-reverse choices keeps the important ones findable.
items.reflection: Pick a decision in your own life that you would want written down for a future version of yourself, and one you would not. What separated them?

items.prompt: A team writes an ADR for every pull request. Six months later nobody reads them. Which principle did they break?
choices: They didn't write them in a template, since that is how it is normally done
They spent the format on decisions that weren't significant or costly to reverse, burying the ones that were
They wrote them in markdown rather than a wiki, regardless of how circumstances develop
They didn't assign a number to each, as most teams assume in practice
items.explanation: Indiscriminate recording defeats findability; the signal drowns in noise.

Yes, because significance includes how much other work will depend on it

items.prompt: A large, high-profile decision is made, but it can be undone with a single configuration flag in minutes. How does that change the case for an ADR?

It removes the need for any discussion, as most teams assume in practice
It makes the decision automatically Accepted, which is the usual convention
It weakens it, since cheap reversal means the cost of being wrong is low
items.explanation: Reversibility matters as much as visibility; cheap to undo means a light process is enough.

items.prompt: A two-way door decision is one that is...
items.explanation: Two-way doors can be walked back through.

items.prompt: A one-way door decision is one that is...
items.explanation: One-way doors are hard to undo.

items.prompt: What should you do with a two-way door decision?
choices: Make the call quickly and adjust if wrong
items.explanation: Cheap reversal means speed beats deliberation.

items.prompt: What should you do with a one-way door decision?
choices: Compare options deliberately and write down why
items.explanation: High reversal cost justifies deliberate comparison and a record.

items.prompt: Migrating the primary datastore is...
items.explanation: It means months of work to reverse.

items.prompt: Trying a new log format for a week is...
items.explanation: You can switch back immediately.

items.prompt: The one-way/two-way test asks...
choices: How expensive is it to undo this?
items.explanation: Reversal cost is the question.

items.prompt: A two-way door decision generally needs...
items.explanation: The ceremony isn't worth it when reversal is cheap.

items.prompt: A team adopts a new code formatter. Two weeks later they dislike it and revert in an afternoon. Was this the right way to handle the decision?
choices: Yes, it was a two-way door and a quick trial was the cheap way to learn
No, they should have written an ADR first, since that is how it is normally done
No, they should have waited a quarter, regardless of how circumstances develop
Yes, but only because formatters are code-style tools, as most teams assume in practice
items.explanation: Fast, low-ceremony trial is correct when reversal is cheap.
items.reference:
🚪 Two-way door — cheap to reverse: decide fast, learn, adjust
🔐 One-way door — expensive to reverse: compare options and write it down
❓ The test — how costly is it to undo if we are wrong?

Why: the care a decision deserves scales with how expensive it is to undo, not with how much people debate it.
items.reflection: List a recent decision of yours that was a two-way door and one that was a one-way door. Did you treat them differently? What would you change?

items.prompt: A team picks a managed queue and, two years in, builds twenty services and tooling around its message format. How has the door changed since the original decision?

It became two-way, since the system is more mature, since that is how it is normally done
It disappeared, since the decision is now old, regardless of how circumstances develop

items.prompt: In a weighted decision matrix, a criterion's weight expresses...
choices: How much it matters to this decision
items.explanation: Weight is importance; score is performance.

items.prompt: A score expresses...
choices: How well an option meets one criterion
items.explanation: Scores rate options against criteria.

items.prompt: How do you get an option's total?
choices: Sum of weight times score across criteria
items.explanation: Total = sum of weight x score.

items.prompt: What does a matrix NOT remove?
items.explanation: Someone still picks criteria and weights.

items.prompt: A big benefit of a matrix is...
items.explanation: People can challenge one number at a time.

items.prompt: If cost weight rises sharply, the cheaper option tends to...
items.explanation: Higher weight on its strength helps it.

items.prompt: Two options tie on total. What does that suggest?
choices: The choice is sensitive to weights and needs more thought
items.explanation: A tie means the weights decide; look closer at them.

items.prompt: Why record the weights in an ADR?
choices: So a reader can see what mattered at the time
items.explanation: The weights are the rationale a reader needs.

items.prompt: Two engineers use identical criteria and scores for two options but get different winners. What is the most likely cause?
choices: They assigned different weights to the criteria
One of them mis-added the totals every time
The options have unequal numbers of criteria
Scores always change between people, since that is how it is normally done
items.explanation: Scores are close to factual once criteria are set; weights are the judgment.
items.reference:
📋 Criteria — what matters for this decision
⚖️ Weights — how much each matters, a judgment call
🔢 Scores — how well each option meets each criterion
➕ Total — sum of weight times score per option

Why: the matrix converts a diffuse argument into specific visible numbers, and the weights are where disagreement now lives.
items.reflection: Consider choosing between two flats, two jobs, or two phones. Which criteria would you weight heavily, and would a friend with different circumstances weight them differently?

items.prompt: A matrix shows Option A ahead 41 to 29, but 80% of A's lead comes from one heavily weighted criterion. What should the ADR say?
choices: Nothing, since A won, regardless of how circumstances develop
That the decision depends on that criterion and should be revisited if it weakens
That A is objectively better, as most teams assume in practice
That the other criteria are irrelevant, which is the usual convention
items.explanation: Stating the dependency tells a future reader which fact to re-check.

The matrix is being reverse-engineered to justify a pre-chosen answer
The criteria will have equal weight, as most teams assume in practice
items.explanation: Criteria and weights should be fixed before totals are known, or the matrix becomes rationalization.

items.prompt: Why not edit the old ADR in place?

items.prompt: A team quietly migrates from RabbitMQ to SQS and edits ADR-014's Decision section to say SQS. What has been lost?
choices: The record that RabbitMQ was chosen, why, and what changed to make it stop fitting
Nothing, since the ADR is now accurate, as most teams assume in practice
The file name of the ADR, which is the usual convention
The ability to compare SQS options, since that is how it is normally done
items.explanation: An accurate-looking edit erases the history a later reader needs.
items.reference:
🆕 New ADR — records the new decision, context, and consequences
🏷️ Old ADR — status flips to Superseded, pointing forward
📚 History — stays intact so the original reasoning is not lost

Why: editing in place erases the history an ADR exists to preserve; superseding keeps both the old reasoning and the reason it changed.

items.explanation: Stale means confidently wrong.

items.prompt: Why can a stale ADR be worse than none?

items.explanation: A missing record prompts questions; a wrong one doesn't.

items.prompt: Which ADR statuses can go stale?
items.explanation: Superseded and Deprecated already say they aren't current.

items.prompt: A time-based trigger is...
choices: A periodic review of old ADRs
items.explanation: Calendar-driven.

items.prompt: An event-based trigger is...
choices: A migration or incident in the decision's area
items.explanation: Something happens that may invalidate the decision.

items.prompt: A change-coupled trigger means...
choices: Code changes in the area must link or update the ADR
items.explanation: It ties the record to the change.

items.prompt: A date on a document is...
choices: Not by itself a trigger to recheck
items.explanation: Someone has to act on it.

items.prompt: What is the cheapest fix for staleness?
choices: Make someone ask 'is this still true?' at a defined moment
items.explanation: A deliberate check is the cure.

items.prompt: A team migrated quietly from RabbitMQ to SQS six months ago and ADR-014 still says Accepted. Which single practice would most likely have prevented this?
choices: A rule that changes to the queueing layer must link or update an ADR in code review
A yearly sweep of all ADRs, which is the usual convention
Longer ADR text, since that is how it is normally done
A bigger review committee, regardless of how circumstances develop
items.explanation: The migration was a code change; coupling the ADR to that change catches the omission when it happens.
items.reference:
⏱️ Time-based — periodic sweep of old Accepted ADRs
⚡ Event-based — incident, migration, or new dependency prompts a check
🔗 Change-coupled — code changes in the area must link or update the ADR

Why: a status field nobody rechecks drifts out of truth; triggers move the check to the moment the decision changes.
items.reflection: Where in your life or work do you rely on a document or list to be current without anything forcing anyone to check? What cheap trigger could you add?
